fields.flaw: Absolute net convergence of the generalized sum indexed over all natural numbers to r implies that the series indexed from n=1 is absolutely convergent to the same value r.
fields.problem:
Title: Absolute Net Convergence Equivalent to Absolute Convergence/Absolute Net Convergence implies Absolute Convergence

Let $V$ be a [[Definition:Banach Space|Banach space]].

Let $\sequence {v_n}_{n \mathop \in \N}$ be a [[Definition:Sequence|sequence]] of elements in $V$.

Let $r \in \R_{\mathop \ge 0}$

Let the [[Definition:Generalized Sum|generalized sum]] $\ds \sum \set {v_n: n \in \N}$ be [[Definition:Absolute Net Convergence|absolutely net convergent]] to $r$.

Then:
:the [[Definition:Series|series]] $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty v_n$ is [[Definition:Absolutely Convergent Series|absolutely convergent]] to $r$.
fields.source_context:
0013 | We have:
0014 | :$\closedint 0 m \supseteq \closedint 0 N \supseteq F$
0015 | 
0016 | From $(1)$:
0017 | :$\size{\ds \sum_{n \mathop \in \closedint 0 m} \norm{v_n} - r} < \epsilon$
0018 | 
0019 | By definition of [[Definition:Summation over Finite Index|summation over finite index]]:
0020 | :$\size{\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^m \norm{v_n} - r} < \epsilon$
0021 | 
0022 | Since $m \ge N$ was arbitrary, it follows that:
0023 | :$\forall m \ge N : \size{\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 0}^m \norm{v_n} - r} < \epsilon$
0024 | 
0025 | Since $\epsilon$ was arbitrary, it follows that the [[Definition:Series|series]] $\ds \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty v_n$ is [[Definition:Absolutely Convergent Series|absolutely convergent]] to $r$ by definition.
0026 | 
0027 | {{qed}}

fields.witness: Let v : ℕ → ℝ be v(0)=1 and v(n)=0 for every n≥1; set r=1. For the net of sums over finite F⊆ℕ, once F contains 0, ∑_{n∈F}v(n)=1. The same holds for ∑|v(n)|, so the generalized sum is absolutely net-convergent to r. The series from n=1 has every term zero, so its norm sum is 0 rather than r=1. This refutes only the same-value claim, not absolute convergence.

scope_metadata.target_scope: The assertion that the tail series starting at 1 has the same absolute sum r as the net over indices including 0; not absolute convergence as a yes/no property.
